lines: This is Sarah.
She works as a pharmacist.
At this morning’s team meeting, her manager said that AI has been around for decades.
Sarah was surprised.
Didn’t all of this start with ChatGPT?
Like many people, Sarah first heard about AI when chat tools appeared in the news.
So let’s travel back in time and see where the story really begins.
In the 1950s, computers filled whole rooms and cost a fortune.
Most were used for calculations.
But some researchers began asking a bigger question: could a computer do things we normally link with human intelligence, like solving problems or using language?
In 1950, the mathematician Alan Turing wrote about this question.
He suggested a test: if you chatted with a machine and couldn’t tell it apart from a person, what would that tell us?
Then, in 1956, researchers gathered for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States.
It was called the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, and the name stuck.
So the term “artificial intelligence” is about seventy years old.
For many years, a popular approach was to give computers rules.
Researchers sat with experts, like doctors or engineers, and wrote down how they made decisions.
Then they turned that knowledge into long lists of “if this, then that” rules.
Imagine a help system for a broken printer.
It asks: is the printer switched on?
If not, switch it on.
If it is, is there paper in the tray?
If not, add paper.
Systems like this, often called expert systems, could be useful for narrow jobs.
But they were also fragile.
Every rule had to be written by hand, the lists grew huge and hard to update, and when something happened that nobody had written a rule for, the system got stuck.
When results fell short of big promises, interest and funding dropped for a while.
People later called these quiet periods “AI winters”.
But the research carried on.
In 1997, a computer called Deep Blue beat by champion Garry Kasparov.
Deep Blue didn’t learn chess the way a person does.
It checked millions of possible moves every second, guided by rules and scoring that people had written.
Over the following years, machine learning.
Instead of writing every rule by hand, people gave computers lots of examples and let them find patterns, like the idea you met in Lesson 1.
Machine learning helped computers get much better recognising speech and making predictions.
That’s how AI found its way into everyday tools.
By the 2010s, AI was already part of daily life.
Lesson 2.
Spam filters, photo search and route suggestions were already using it, often without anyone noticing.
Then, in November 2022, a company called OpenAI released ChatGPT, and similar tools from other…
For the first time, almost anyone could type a question in plain words and get a written reply on almost any topic.
People could talk to AI directly.
AI wasn’t new.
What changed was how visible and easy to use it became.
So, did AI start with ChatGPT?
No.
It grew from decades of work: big questions in the 1950s, rule-based systems, quiet periods when progress stalled, and the rise of…
…is one recent chapter in a much longer story.
Back at work, Sarah smiles.
AI has been around for decades.
It just became much easier to see.
Next, we’ll look at how to tell AI apart from ordinary software.
